content.summary_of_the_paper: The submission states that it proposes two novel algorithms for two-player zero-sum Markov games. The submission performs experiments in both tabular games and video games and compares to relevant baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Disingenuity 

I feel, unfortunately, that the authors may be engaging disingenuously with the peer review process. I previously reviewed this submission for NeurIPS. While I did not bid for this submission, I was assigned it a second time for ICLR. In the NeurIPS submission process, the authors were given many constructive criticisms. Chiefly among these was the existence of very related work that was not discussed. I have posted the discussion with the authors regarding this work below.

```
Reviewer comment: I am making a separate post because I realized that I overlooked the fact that the submission missed important related work:
No-Press Diplomacy from Scratch (NeurIPS 2021)
See, in particular, the section on Deep Nash Value Iteration.
While this approach is model-based, it is otherwise quite similar to the submission. Unfortunately, I feel that it serves much of the purpose that the submission might have in literature. Thus, independent of other issues, I feel now that the submission would be a bit borderline.

—

Author response: We would like to thank the reviewer for pointing out the missing reference [1]. We agree that [1] is very related to our work, and we will add this reference to the paper and discuss the difference and similarity. Here, we would like to emphasize several differences that highlight our contribution compared to [1].
1. The targeted environment is different. [1] focuses on Diplomacy games, while this paper focuses on Atari games. Both environments have unique structures that result in many differences between their algorithms and ours in terms of the implementation details, and the use of practical tricks. To our best knowledge, our paper is the first one that finds hard-to-exploit policies (with empirical justifications) in video games such as two-player Atari games.
2. We compared our algorithm with existing algorithms such as PSRO/fictitious play/self-play, and showed the superiority of our methods in both tabular environments and Atari games, while [1] did not do such comparison.
3. In addition to the difference in details, as pointed out by the reviewer, the algorithm proposed in [1] is model-based which requires knowing the transition, while our algorithm is model-free.
In summary, we believe the main contribution of this paper is NOT to propose a brand new algorithm (in fact, we mentioned this throughout the paper that the algorithm is a deep version of existing tabular algorithms), but to (i) implement a practical algorithm and make it hard to exploit in two-player Atari games and to (ii) outperform existing algorithms such as PSRO/fictitious play. We believe neither of these two main contributions is covered in [1].
Reference:
[1] No-Press Diplomacy from Scratch (NeurIPS 2021)

—

Reviewer comment: I appreciate the authors taking the time to look over this paper.
While I do not disagree with the authors' characterization in 1. and 2., I am not sure they are such a strong argument.
1. [1] achieved superhuman performance for an actively researched game for which superhuman AI did not previously exist. Simply performing experiments on different domains does not add that much value.
2. It's true that [1] does not compare against baselines, but given that the game had an active research community and no previous AI had achieved superhuman performance, I feel confident that PSRO/FP would not have performed as well.
3. I think this is the authors' strongest point.
Overall, I am not asserting that there is categorically not room in literature for the submission. However, given the relative lack of novelty (specifically, the existence of both tabular and model-based variants of its algorithm), I think it is especially important that
i. The submission does a good job informing the reader of the context of the literature.
ii. The submission provides empirical results with high certainty.
For point i), I really still feel that it is important that the submission has both an extensive related work (front and center, not in the appendix) and a background section that actually provides the reader with requisite understanding of tabular algorithm the submission is building on (again, front and center, not in the appendix). For point ii), I think it would help to use more than three seeds, as the level of certainty in the results from three seeds is not very high.
```
The authors state that the work is “very related” and that they would “add this reference to the paper and discuss the difference and similarity”. However, in the current submission, there is no reference to [1]. Indeed, the submission states “There has not been much prior empirical efforts to design algorithms specializing in solving zero-sum MGs” despite the fact that, as evidenced by the above transcript, the authors were made aware of such existing work.

### Comments


> Different from prior efforts on training agents to beat a fixed set of opponents, our objective is to find the Nash equilibrium policies that are free from exploitation by even the adversarial opponents

This is a strange way to put it. There are many works concerned with finding Nash equilibrium policies (most of which are not acknowledged by the submission). I don’t think the submission benefits from framing exploitability as a novel pursuit.

> Distinct from EFGs which feature tree-structured transition dynamics and do not efficiently represent the games where multiple states in the past may lead to the same state in the future, this paper focuses on MGs with general transition structure, and leverages the Markov structures.

EFGs are more general than MGs in terms of the information structures that they can naturally capture. This sentence seems to suggest the opposite. There is no need for the submission to make this kind of misleading insinuation — Markov games are perfectly worth studying. (I understand that representational efficiency may be important for tabular convergence rates, but it is not a primary issue for deep RL.)

> Another line of prior works (Heinrich & Silver, 2016; Lanctot et al., 2017) directly combine the best-response-based algorithm for finding NE in normal-form games, such as fictitious play (Brown, 1951) and double oracle (McMahan et al., 2003), with single-agent deep RL algorithm such as DQN (Mnih et al., 2013) and PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) for finding the best-response.

The submission seems to contrast these works to the works cited earlier in the paragraph. Yet McAleer 2021 uses the best response oracle discussed here.

> More importantly, comparing to MGs, the model of IIEFGs made a strong assumption of transition which must be tree-formed. The results of IIEFG typically scales super-linearly with respect to the number of information sets, which in general grows exponentially with the horizon length of the game.

Again, the submission seems concerned with claiming some superiority of MGs over IIEFGs, which is not appropriate here. Furthermore, the authors cite works Kozuno et al. (2021) that are concerned with POSGs, which are straightforwardly generalizations of MGs.

> Among those, Nash Q-learning (Hu & Wellman, 2003) is one of
the earliest works along this line of research, which provably converges to NE for general-sum games under the assumption that the NE is unique for each stage game during the learning process. On the
other hand, GOLF_WITH_EXPLOITER (Jin et al., 2021b) is another theoretical work with provable
polynomial convergence for two-player zero-sum MGs. Our NASH_DQN algorithm is designed
based on the provable tabular algorithm Nash Value Iteration (Liu et al., 2021), which is a natural
extension of value iteration algorithm from single-agent setting to the multi-agent setting.

I don't feel that this paragraph sufficiently clarifies why the algorithms in the paper are designed based on Liu et al. (2021), rather than Hu & Wellman (2003). Liu et al. propose a model-based algorithm, whereas, like Hu & Wellman (2003), the algorithms in the submission are model free. I think this is an important point for the clarity of the submission. It was also raised by *multiple reviewers* in the previous submission cycle.

> Nash Q-Learning (Hu & Wellman, 2003) is the model-free version of NASH_VI.

This is a strange way of framing it -- Hu & Wellman (2003) is an older and more well-established than Nash VI.

### Background section

As it stands, I do not feel that the background section is structured appropriately. The most important part of the background section (informing the readers about the details of the tabular algorithms the submission builds upon) is afforded a mere few lines. This issue was also raised in the previous review cycle.

### Other relevant related work / baselines

The submissions misses a few classes of related work for minimizing exploitability with deep reinforcement learning. One class scales counterfactual regret minimization:
- Deep Counterfactual Regret Minimization (ICML 2019)
- Double Neural Counterfactual Regret Minimization (ICLR 2020)
- DREAM: Deep Regret minimization with Advantage baselines and Model-free learning
- The Advantage Regret-Matching Actor-Critic
- ESCHER: Eschewing Importance Sampling in Games by Computing a History Value Function to Estimate Regret

Another class uses regularization to induce convergence:
- From Poincaré Recurrence to Convergence in Imperfect Information Games: Finding Equilibrium via Regularization (ICML 2021)
- A Unified Approach to Reinforcement Learning, Quantal Response Equilibria, and Two-Player Zero-Sum Games

A third class uses public belief states:
- Combining Deep Reinforcement Learning and Search for Imperfect-Information Games (NeurIPS 2020)
- Player of Games

While I am not suggesting that the submission need necessarily compare against them, the way the submission is currently written makes it seem as if best response oracle-based approaches are the only major existing class of algorithms for minimizing exploitability with deep RL, which is not the case.

### Experiments

> Table 1

There is no uncertainty quantification here. Is this just one seed?

> Fig. 3 and Table 2 show the exploitation results of all algorithms and baselines. Each method is trained for three random seeds ... For each method and environment, Table 2 displays the best performing models with its corresponding exploitability. 

In my opinion, three seeds is not sufficient for a paper whose primary contribution (in my opinion) is empirical benchmarking. Furthermore, in my opinion, displaying the best seed for each method is not appropriate. Also, what notion of uncertainty is used to draw the bands in Figure 2? Lastly, the way the bands are drawn makes it hard to tell how large they are. (Same comment for figure 5.)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As articulated above, the submission is lacking in various particulars of quality, clarity, and originality.
content.summary_of_the_review: On top of numerous other issues articulated above, I feel that the authors may be engaging disingenuously with peer review.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3162 by Reviewer ja4M

content.title: Brief response
content.comment:
-Disingenuity:

We disagree with the reviewer's claim of disingenuity of the paper for the following reasons:
1. When we wrote the original version of the paper, we were completely unaware of this paper (No-Press Diplomacy from Scratch), and did not borrow anything from that paper.
2. There are many changes made after the NeurIPS submission, and we admit that we are aware of the paper after the reviewer mentioned the paper in the rebuttal phase. It's our mistake that we missed the reference after the review, and we want to emphasize that we didn't intentionally leaving this reference out.
3. As noticed by the reviewers, our main contribution is in experiment. For these two papers, the experimental environments, comparing algorithms and results are significantly different. To our current understanding, they have not shown non-exploitable performances of the learning agents in their experiments while we showed non-exploitability at least under the limited capacity of the exploiter.

-EFGs are more general than MGs in terms of the information structures that they can naturally capture. This sentence seems to suggest the opposite. (I understand that representational efficiency may be important for tabular convergence rates, but it is not a primary issue for deep RL.)

We strongly disagree with the claim that representational efficiency is not a primary issue for Deep RL.
To use EFGs to represent a graph structured (not tree structured) transition, it needs an exponential number of duplicated states, which leads to significant inefficiency. Running any EFG algorithm on Markov games will lead to sample/computational complexity that’s prohibitive in practice.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors consider two-player zero-sum games and present deep-RL-based algorithms for finding Nash equilibria in such games. These are Q-learning-based algorithms, that is, they work by approximating action-value functions for the players. They are essentially deep-RL-ified versions of existing algorithms from the literature. The authors demonstrate success compared to baselines on a variety of "toy" games and more complex Atari games.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: the topic is of obvious importance, the empirical evaluations seem solid, the approaches are clearly explained. The results seem to outperform baselines that I believe to be reasonable.

Weaknesses: 

Some of the claims seem unreasonably strong, for instance "This is to our knowledge the first work for learning non-exploitable strategies in two-player zero-sum video games like Atari" seems like it cannot be right -- finding non-exploitable strategies in 2-player zero sum games just means finding a Nash equilibrium, and there are many previous works that aim to do this via deep RL (including the baselines in the paper). Elsewhere in the paper the authors distinguish between their own work, which takes advantage of the Markov game structure, and other work which basically assumes a normal-form game where actions are policies, but this difference seems very subtle compared to their strong claim of novelty. I hope the authors can clarify this during the response period and either explain why I'm wrong or weaken the claims in the paper.

Question for authors: The Nash-DQN algorithm is based on Nash-VI, but then seems to throw away the model based approach of Nash-VI (doesn't estimate the transition probabilities). In this case, what are the differences between Nash DQN and classic Nash Q-learning?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: the paper is reasonably clear in presenting what it actually did, although presentations of related work could be stronger.

Novelty: the main novelty of the paper seems to be empirical, i.e. it's taking theoretically-proven algorithms for finding Nash equilibria and extending them to the deep RL setting, in the same way that the general idea of Q-learning can be modified by adding replay buffer, function approximation, exploration strategies, etc.. It is unclear how different these approaches are from existing Q-learning approaches in the literature.

Quality: the quality seems to be fairly high, empirical evaluations are carefully done and not just on toy environments, etc.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think it is an okay paper which presents reasonable empirical results for some nice algorithms. I have some concerns about the novelty which I think it is possible for the authors to address in their rebuttal.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Brief response
content.comment:
-Finding non-exploitable strategies in 2-player zero sum games just means finding a Nash equilibrium, and there are many previous works.

Most previous works including the baseline methods are designed for extensive-form games but not Markov games, and it's known that those methods are not sample efficient for Markov games at least in tabular cases. By the time we submitted the paper, we are not aware of any other work on the two-player Atari games (Markov game) for achieving a Nash equilibrium.

-Differences between Nash DQN and classic Nash Q-learning 

Sec. B.11 in appendix very clearly discusses the difference of Nash DQN, Nash Q-learning, Nash VI, etc. And we didn't draw any conclusion on Nash DQN is function approximation of Nash VI or Nash Q-learning, it's similar to both for different reasons. We feel it meaningless to keep arguing about whether the algorithm A is closer to B or C on different aspects.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes Nash DQN algorithms for finding the Nash equilibrium policies for two-player zero-sum Markov games. The proposed algorithms are practical implementations of theoretical algorithms that are guaranteed to converge to Nash equilibrium under the tabular setting. Moreover, the experimental evaluations show that the proposed Nash DQN algorithms can find policies free from adversarial opponents on tabular examples and several two-player Atari games.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
This paper proposes Nash DQN algorithm and Nash DQN Exploiter algorithm. The proposed algorithms have been both theoretically and empirically proven to find approximate Nash equilibria in finite steps with a definite minimal probability in the tabular settings. The algorithms have also been extended to use neural networks as function approximators. The empirical result shows that the algorithms can defend the adversarial exploiters.

Weaknesses:
The analysis in the paper is mainly about exploitability. For Atari games, the exploitability is measured from the trained exploiter against each trained model. However, comparing the real strength of playing games is also essential besides the exploitability. Therefore, the authors should also provide the results between the Nash DQN algorithms and other algorithms rather than only the exploiters. Furthermore, the baseline methods should also include recent SOTA DRL algorithms for Atari games (e.g., Agent57, R2D2, MuZero, NGU). Finally, the authors should demonstrate whether an exploiter can easily exploit other SOTA algorithms.
On the other hand, the high time complexity of the proposed algorithms is a concern. The authors should compare the results based on the number of training steps, the total training time, the required computing resources, or other comparable metrics. For example, given the same computing resources, compare the learning performance between Nash DQN and other baseline methods.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The authors claim that this work is the first for learning non-exploitable strategies in two-player zero-sum video games like Atari. However, justifying this point requires more clarification about why previous works did not achieve it. To be more specific, for example, given the same conditions (e.g., RAM-based Atari, truncating to 300 steps, 5x10^4 training episodes, etc.) for learning, why are previous algorithms incapable of learning non-exploitable strategies in Atari environments? For reproducibility, this paper provides sufficient materials, including source code and hyperparameters.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes Nash DQN algorithms for two-player zero-sum and applies them to video games like Atari. It seems to be the first work for learning non-exploitable strategies in such environments; however, the authors should be more specific in comparing related works and provide more experimental evaluations to justify the effectiveness in practice.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3162 by Reviewer uC64

content.title: Brief response
content.comment:
-To include recent SOTA DRL algorithms for Atari games

It's a good suggestion to involve the experiments for previous SOTA Atari algorithms, which we will try to add later. However, with some game-theoretical knowledge it should be easily known that single-agent DRL algorithms designed for solving MDP only will be insufficient to provide non-exploitable strategies. In rock-paper-scissor game the pure strategy of playing rock is optimal against playing purely scissor, but it has nothing to do with non-exploitability. If we also implement other SOTA DRL algorithms, the reviewers can further ask why not combine Nash-DQN with those SOTA DRL algorithms, afterall most of the techniques in SOTA DRL algorithms would be independent of the Nash methods. Our choice is to provide the vanilla version of the algorithm, which demonstrates the function approximatioin generalization of theoretical justified algorithms in a most clear and compact way.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: Using five two-player Atari environments and the SlimeVolley environment, this paper proposes two DQN-variant algorithm for learning equilibrium and non-exploitable strategies. This is compared against self-play and other baselines, with improved performance (lower exploitability) of the proposed algorithms.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- Designing strategies that are not exploitable (i.e., perform well against opponents that seek to minimize one's own payoff) in two-player games is an important area.
- Incorporating game-theoretic concepts into designing Deep RL algorithms is a relatively novel direction that will likely prove to be increasingly important in both competitive settings, as described in this paper, and in cooperative domains.
- The discussion of solvers in the appendix is unusual to include but could actually be quite beneficial to others seeking to do empirical/practical work in this domain.

Weaknesses
- The empirical evaluation is not sufficient. Table 2 is not clear and there should be at least some mention of absolute scores obtained by agents. This omission makes the claims difficult to evaluate.
- Training for ~10,000 episodes in Atari is likely not sufficient for learning much, at least without substantial pre-training. What the curves in Figure 3 intend to demonstrate is not entirely clear.
- Training Atari using RAM (as opposed to pixels) is definitely not standard -- there are limited results on how effective RAM-based training is, and likely has a very significant impact on performance of policies; 300 time steps is also a very short time duration for episodes, especially in Double Dunk and Surround, and possibly Boxing.
- While this may be a minor point, the title of the paper includes "Two-Player Atari Games" but one of the six domains used is not an Atari game. Not certain what better phrasing would be, but I would suggest a different title if possible.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity of the paper in terms of the experimental results is not sufficient. While this paper proposes a variation on DQN that is "less exploitable", it is not clear how exploitation strategies are developed, and how well this generalizes. DQN also requires much more training time to get anything beyond random performance, and it's not convincing that using RAM alleviates this problem.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the paper presents some interesting results, the main weaknesses are in the significance of the empirical results. These are not sufficient to be convincing; the experimental evidence needs to be presented in a more thorough and systematic way, including scores.

content.title: Brief response
content.comment:
-The empirical evaluation is not sufficient.

The Table 2 actually shows just the average episodic reward of the exploiter agent at the end of training, and the reward of the fixed agents are the inverse.

-The 10000 episodes training, RAM observation and 300 time steps.

These choices are compatible with the affordable computational budgets. 300 time steps may be short, but it should be sufficient to show some necessary strategies in most of the games. For games like Boxing, Double Dunk, there is strong time homogeneity at different time scales (but fewer than 300 steps), we are not expecting the game with full episode length to have much different strategies.
